headline: A forgotten recording town, and a sound the Hornets can claim
summary: Charlotte's music story is mostly untold. It was an early country-recording hub, and James Brown cut a hit here in 1965. The Hive's sellout years share a moment with Jodeci's hip-hop soul, and the rap bench is quietly deep. Build a "Cut in Charlotte" sound with paid local partners instead of hip-hop clichés borrowed from other cities.

insights.title: Charlotte cut records before Nashville did
insights.detail: WBT signed on in 1922, and its Briarhoppers string band ruled 1930s Carolina radio. RCA's Bluebird label ran field sessions in Uptown in 1936-38, where the Monroe Brothers made their first records. Arthur Smith's "Guitar Boogie" and "Feudin' Banjos" (later "Dueling Banjos") came out of Charlotte. James Brown recorded 'Papa's Got a Brand New Bag' at Arthur Smith Studios in 1965.
insights.implication: Tell a "Cut in Charlotte" story with liner notes, 78-rpm label type and radio-dial graphics. No other NBA market has this heritage, and few locals know it. License the artist names, recordings and label marks first.

insights.title: The Hive and hip-hop soul are one memory
insights.detail: The Hornets sold out 364 straight games at the 24,000-seat Charlotte Coliseum as Larry Johnson and Alonzo Mourning arrived in 1991-92. That is the moment Charlotte's Jodeci released "Forever My Lady" and helped invent hip-hop soul. Charlotte-born Anthony Hamilton carried the lineage into the 2000s with "Comin' from Where I'm From".
insights.implication: Make teal throwbacks sound like early-90s Charlotte R&B, not generic 90s nostalgia. Soundtrack them with Hamilton or a licensed Jodeci moment. Aim at fans aged 35-50 who wore the Starter jackets the first time.

insights.title: Rap's biggest local name carries baggage, but the bench is deep
insights.detail: DaBaby, raised in Charlotte, landed a No. 1 album ("Kirk", 2019) and a No. 1 single ("Rockstar", 2020). He lost festival slots after homophobic remarks at Rolling Loud in 2021. The respected local voices are Lute of J. Cole's Dreamville ("West1996", "Gold Mouf"), MAVI ("Let the Sun Talk") and Reuben Vincent of 9th Wonder's Jamla.
insights.implication: Build credited, paid collaborations with Lute, MAVI or Reuben Vincent. Keep DaBaby out of any lead role. This city lost the 2017 All-Star Game over the HB2 "bathroom bill", so inclusion is not optional.

insights.title: The West End's sound is brass and drums
insights.detail: Johnson C. Smith University on Beatties Ford Road fields the International Institute of Sound marching band. From 2006 to 2020 the CIAA Tournament filled Charlotte's arena and clubs every February with step shows and concerts, before it moved to Baltimore. Up the road, the 1944 Excelsior Club hosted touring Black stars until it closed in 2016.
insights.implication: Co-design an HBCU-night or CIAA-week capsule with JCSU: band braid, drumhead graphics, navy and gold. Pay the band and route proceeds to its music program. The look should come from the band, not be costumed by Nike.

insights.title: 'Raise Up' is the state's crowd ritual
insights.detail: Greenville rapper Petey Pablo's 2001 "Raise Up" ('North Carolina, come on and raise up... spin it like a helicopter') is still the shirt-twirling anthem at Carolinas stadiums. Coby White, from Goldsboro in eastern NC and a former Tar Heel, re-signed this summer as part of the new core.
insights.implication: Build a helicopter rally towel or a twist-to-read tee on the "raise up" gesture. Front it with a homegrown player like White, if he is a Nike athlete, and clear it with the song's rights holders. Nike can own that crowd ritual.

insights.title: The team's soundtrack is up for grabs
insights.detail: Charlotte's 2019 NBA All-Star Game put Carolinas artists on the Spectrum Center floor (performer lineup to be confirmed). Fayetteville's J. Cole and Charlotte's Anthony Hamilton are the state's best-known voices. The LaMelo Ball era and its Puma-driven content are over, and the team now belongs to Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel.
insights.implication: During the reset, commission a Charlotte producer and a local artist-in-residence for intros, hype videos and drop soundtracks. First confirm which player faces aren't contracted to rival brands (Miller has been a Puma athlete).

insights.title: The Carolinas gave jazz its giants
insights.detail: Four giants were born inside the Hornets' two-state territory: John Coltrane (Hamlet, NC), Thelonious Monk (Rocky Mount), Dizzy Gillespie (Cheraw, SC) and Nina Simone (Tryon, NC). Charlotte-born Romare Bearden made jazz and blues the subject of collages such as his "Of the Blues" series. Uptown's Romare Bearden Park carries his name.
insights.implication: A Bearden-licensed collage graphic or a "Carolinas jazz" story can carry a premium, adult capsule with real roots. Work through the Romare Bearden Foundation and the musicians' estates. Don't imitate the style.

places.name: Neighborhood Theatre
places.why: A converted movie house at the center of the NoDa arts district, and the mid-size room local acts graduate to.

places.name: Snug Harbor
places.why: A pirate-themed dive where indie bands, dance nights and drag share a stage. It's where Plaza Midwood's scene actually hangs out.

places.name: Lunchbox Records
places.why: The independent vinyl shop that carries local releases. A natural pickup point for a numbered, record-style product drop.

places.name: The Milestone Club
places.why: A punk dive open since 1969, where R.E.M. played early shows. It's the city's DIY credential.

places.name: Visulite Theatre
places.why: An intimate room in a historic storefront theater, and a reliable stop for touring and Carolinas acts since 1999.

places.name: The Fillmore Charlotte at AvidXchange Music Factory
places.why: The main mid-size touring hub. It shares a campus with The Underground and Skyla Credit Union Amphitheatre.

places.name: Johnson C. Smith University
places.why: Home of the International Institute of Sound band, and anchor of the Beatties Ford corridor's Black music heritage.

places.name: Camp North End
places.why: A 1924 Ford assembly plant turned arts, food and music campus, where Charlotte's younger creative scene gathers. A good launch site.

places.name: Romare Bearden Park
places.why: Named for the Charlotte-born collage artist whose work is steeped in jazz and blues. A short walk from Spectrum Center.

places.name: Earl Scruggs Center
places.why: It honors the banjo innovator from nearby Flint Hill, and roots the Hornets' wider-Carolinas fan base in bluegrass history.

people.name: Anthony Hamilton
people.role: Charlotte-born soul singer ("Charlene", "Comin' from Where I'm From")
people.why: The most respected living voice of Charlotte R&B, and the natural lead for any Hive-era or anthem-night campaign.

people.name: Jodeci
people.role: Charlotte R&B quartet (K-Ci, JoJo, DeVante Swing, Mr. Dalvin)
people.why: They defined early-90s hip-hop soul during the Hornets' sellout run. Their name, likeness and recordings need licensing.

people.name: Lute
people.role: West Charlotte rapper signed to J. Cole's Dreamville
people.why: He raps about Charlotte's West Side with Dreamville credibility, a strong fit for a credited local collab.

people.name: MAVI
people.role: Charlotte rapper ("Let the Sun Talk", "Laughing So Hard, It Hurts")
people.why: A critics' favorite with literary, hometown-rooted lyrics. Younger Charlotte fans rep him as the rising voice.

people.name: DaBaby
people.role: Charlotte-raised rapper; founder of Billion Dollar Baby Entertainment
people.why: The city's biggest commercial rap star, and a reputational risk since 2021. Know him, but don't build around him.

people.name: International Institute of Sound (JCSU)
people.role: Johnson C. Smith University marching band
people.why: The West End's living HBCU band tradition, and the obvious paid partner for a drumline, band-braid or CIAA-week night.

people.name: Arthur Smith (1921-2014)
people.role: Guitarist, TV host and studio owner ("Guitar Boogie", "Feudin' Banjos")
people.why: He turned Charlotte into a recording hub. James Brown cut 'Papa's Got a Brand New Bag' in his studio.

people.name: Luke Combs
people.role: Country star born in Huntersville and raised in Asheville
people.why: He co-headlined the October 2024 Concert for Carolina for Helene relief with Eric Church. He's the face of the region's country audience, alongside Concord's Avett Brothers.

moments.name: Hornets home opener
moments.why: The first Spectrum Center night of the Miller-Knueppel era. Debut a new game-night sound and a music-led drop.

moments.name: JCSU Homecoming
moments.why: The International Institute of Sound's biggest showcase on Beatties Ford Road, and a West End gathering for alumni.

moments.name: CIAA Tournament week
moments.why: Charlotte's Black music and party week from 2006 to 2020. Whether or not it returns, it's the template for an HBCU basketball-and-music night.

moments.name: MerleFest
moments.why: The Carolinas' flagship roots festival since 1988, named for Doc Watson's son Merle. It reaches western-NC Hornets fans.

moments.name: Charlotte Pride Festival & Parade
moments.why: Uptown's largest summer street festival. After HB2, visible and credited inclusion work matters here.

moments.name: Festival in the Park
moments.why: A neighborhood arts-and-music festival since 1964. A quiet preseason window to seed product with local makers.

vocabulary.meaning: The Hornets' rallying name for the team and city since the Hornets name returned in 2014.
The old Charlotte Coliseum of the 1988-2002 sellout years. Now it names any loud Hornets crowd.
Charlotte's nickname, after Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. The crown motif comes from it.
Charlotte's area code, repped by local rappers and on merch (980 is the overlay).
What Charlotteans call downtown, and home of Spectrum Center. Say "downtown" and you mark yourself an outsider.
Petey Pablo's 2001 NC anthem. It's also the cue to twist your shirt around your head and spin it like a helicopter.
The Carolinas' swing dance to beach music. It's South Carolina's state dance and North Carolina's official popular dance.
Carolinas shorthand for the R&B and soul records played at coastal pavilions and shag clubs. It isn't surf rock.

designCues.cue: Hornets teal as the hero color for anything Hive-era or hip-hop-soul, paired with Hornets purple #1D1160
designCues.source: The 1988 palette by North Carolina designer Alexander Julian. It's the color of the sold-out Hive and early-90s Charlotte R&B.
designCues.use: Lead throwback and R&B-campaign product with teal and purple. Team colors and marks run through NBA Properties.

designCues.source: JCSU's navy-and-gold International Institute of Sound uniforms on Beatties Ford Road
designCues.use: Use it for soutache-style trim and drumhead roundels on a JCSU co-designed capsule. Treat the hex as a working value and match JCSU's official gold.

designCues.cue: Cut-paper collage layering with torn edges and flat color blocks
designCues.source: Charlotte-born Romare Bearden's jazz and blues collages, such as the "Of the Blues" series
designCues.use: License through the Romare Bearden Foundation, or commission Charlotte collage artists for a layered shooting-shirt print. Never trace or mimic Bearden's compositions.

designCues.cue: 1930s radio and 78-rpm label lettering: condensed deco caps, dial arcs, a circular "label" neck print
designCues.source: WBT's early broadcast era and the 1936-38 Bluebird sessions in Uptown
designCues.use: Draw original lettering for a "Cut in Charlotte" collection. Avoid the RCA and Bluebird marks, which belong to a major label.

designCues.cue: Liner-notes tracklist back print: "Recorded in Charlotte, NC" with years and credits
designCues.source: Charlotte's recording timeline: Monroe Brothers (1936), "Guitar Boogie", 'Papa's Got a Brand New Bag' (1965), Jodeci (1991)
designCues.use: Set it as a tracklist on a warmup back or hang-tag booklet. Clear every artist name and song title with rights holders first.

designCues.cue: Oversized early-90s hip-hop-soul silhouette: drop shoulders, boxy satin and nylon, baggy shorts
designCues.source: Jodeci-era Charlotte R&B styling (oversized denim, leather, combat boots, backwards caps) during the Hive's sellout run
designCues.use: Reference the era, not the group's likeness, in teal-and-purple warmup jackets. Use the group only under license.

designCues.cue: Helicopter-spin graphic printed to read when the shirt is twisted around the head
designCues.source: The "Raise Up" stadium ritual across North Carolina
designCues.use: Rally towels and giveaway tees. Partner with Petey Pablo and pay him, rather than printing the lyric unlicensed.

productHooks: 'Cut in Charlotte' City capsule: a warmup jacket and shooting shirt with a liner-notes back print and a 78-label neck graphic. Sell it as a numbered run through Lunchbox Records, with a 7-inch or playlist from Lute, MAVI or Reuben Vincent. Launch at the Neighborhood Theatre.
HBCU-night or CIAA-week capsule co-designed with JCSU's International Institute of Sound: navy-and-gold band-braid warmups, a drumline pregame, and proceeds to JCSU's music program.

Hive-era R&B throwback drop in teal and purple satin, fronted by Anthony Hamilton (anthem plus campaign). Tie it to Converse heritage: Larry Johnson's "Grandmama" ads were for Converse, now part of Nike.
'Raise Up' Carolinas Night: helicopter rally towels and twist-to-read tees, led by a homegrown player such as Coby White if he is a Nike athlete. Pay Petey Pablo and clear the rights.
Premium "Carolinas Jazz" capsule: a collage-print hoodie and knit, licensed from the Romare Bearden Foundation for adult fans. Sell it at Spectrum Center and Uptown museum shops.
watchouts: DaBaby is Charlotte's biggest commercial rapper, but his 2021 Rolling Loud remarks about gay people and HIV cost him festival slots. Charlotte also lost the 2017 All-Star Game over HB2. Give him no lead role without a full review.
Brandon Miller has been a Puma athlete, and LaMelo Ball (now in Minnesota) was Puma. Confirm Miller's, Knueppel's and Coby White's deals before any player-artist content.
Clear licensing first. That covers James Brown's and Jodeci's names and recordings, Petey Pablo's "Raise Up" lyric, Romare Bearden's art, the RCA/Bluebird label marks and all Hornets/NBA marks.

Tell the story of West End Black music with JCSU, West End groups and the artists themselves, credited and paid. That includes the Excelsior Club and the Brooklyn neighborhood razed by 1960s urban renewal. Don't reduce it to nostalgia graphics.
Beach music and the shag grew from Black R&B records played at segregated Carolina beach pavilions. If product touches that nostalgia, credit the Black originators.
